chapter.name: Turning Tides: 11th and 12th Centuries
chapter.blurb: The Ghaznavid invasions, al-Biruni and Bhaskaracharya, eastern India and the Deccan, Kakatiyas, Hoysalas, Cholas, Paramaras, Ghurids and the culture of the period.

concepts.name: The Ghaznavid invasions
concepts.description: The Hindu Shahis and the Khyber Pass, Mahmud of Ghazni's campaigns, Mathura and Somnath, and their impact.
concepts.idea: Mahmud of Ghazni raided north India repeatedly for plunder and did not set up lasting rule.
concepts.rule: The Hindu Shahis, who controlled the Khyber Pass, resisted invasions for a time. The Turkic Ghaznavids, with capital Ghazna (Ghazni), overran them: Mahmud defeated Jayapala and in 1008 Anandapala despite help from other north Indian rulers. Mahmud took the title of sultan, meaning authority or power, and conducted 17 campaigns in India, returning to Ghazni with booty each time. In 1018 he sacked wealthy Mathura and looted Kannauj; in 1026 he destroyed the Somnath temple in Saurashtra. Salar Masud was defeated by Suheldev at Bahraich according to tradition. Mahmud's campaigns involved plunder, killing of civilians and capture of prisoners sold as slaves. He did not try to establish a permanent base beyond Punjab. The current Somnath temple was built in 1950 with public donations. Al-Biruni recorded the impact on Indian sciences.
concepts.example: The Khyber Pass was a major trade route for at least 2,500 years and an entry for invaders.

concepts.name: Al-Biruni and Bhaskaracharya: scholars of the age
concepts.description: Al-Biruni's survey of India and Bhaskaracharya's mathematical works.
concepts.idea: Al-Biruni studied India's knowledge, and Bhaskaracharya advanced mathematics and astronomy.
concepts.rule: Abu Rayhan al-Biruni, a Persian scholar from Khwarizm in present-day Uzbekistan, was a mathematician, astronomer, geographer, historian and linguist. Around 1017 he accompanied Mahmud to India, learned Sanskrit and read Indian texts, and produced an encyclopaedic survey of Indian religion, philosophy, literature, geography and sciences, comparing them with Greek and Islamic traditions. He collected the work of Aryabhata, Varahamihira and Brahmagupta and translated Patanjali's Yogasutras into Arabic. He noted that Indian sciences retreated from conquered regions to Kashmir, Varanasi and other places. Bhaskaracharya, a great mathematician and astronomer of the 12th century, wrote Lilavati (riddles and problems), Bijaganita (algebra) and Siddhanta Shiromani (astronomy). His works were translated into Persian and Europe rediscovered some of his techniques centuries later.
concepts.example: Lilavati teaches mathematics through lively riddles and problems.

concepts.name: Eastern India and the Deccan: Senas, Eastern Gangas and Chalukyas
concepts.description: The Senas and Jayadeva, the Eastern Gangas of Kalinga, and the decline of the Western Chalukyas.
concepts.idea: In the east, the Senas and Eastern Gangas rose while the Western Chalukyas faded.
concepts.rule: After the Palas declined, the Sena dynasty became dominant in Bengal with capital Nadiya. Unlike the Palas who patronised Buddhism, the Senas promoted Hindu thought and literature and hosted the poet Jayadeva, author of the Gitagovindam about Krishna and Radha. The Eastern Gangas of Kalinga (Odisha) had marital alliances with the Cholas and also clashed with them; by the end of the 12th century their kingdom stretched from the Ganga to the Godavari. The Western Chalukyas ruled from Kalyani and were a major Deccan power reaching the Narmada. Fierce Chola-Western Chalukya wars over Vengi caused the Western Chalukyas to fade and the Kakatiyas and Hoysalas to replace them.
concepts.example: The Konark Sun temple is linked to the Eastern Gangas.

concepts.name: The Kakatiyas and the Hoysalas
concepts.description: The Kakatiyas of Warangal and the Hoysalas of Karnataka, their administration, literature and temples.
concepts.idea: The Kakatiyas built forts, irrigation and the Thousand Pillar temple, and the Hoysalas built famed temples.
concepts.rule: In the 12th century the Kakatiyas consolidated authority over much of Telangana and Andhra Pradesh from Orugallu (Warangal), where they built a fort with stone gateways (toranas). Some kings wrote Sanskrit works and they patronised Telugu literature; the Thousand Pillar temple at Hanamkonda is a fine example of their architecture. They promoted village self-governance, an efficient revenue system and irrigation. The Hoysalas began in southern Karnataka; legend says the name comes from an ascetic's command 'Poy, Sala' meaning 'strike, Sala'. Their capitals were Velapura (Belur) and Dvarasamudra (Halebidu). Under Vishnuvardhana they broke from Chalukya overlordship and challenged the Cholas. Their temples at Belur and Halebidu, with intricately carved pillars and panels, are UNESCO World Heritage monuments.
concepts.example: The Hoysala temple at Somanathapura shows elaborate statues and friezes.

concepts.name: The Cholas, masters of the seas
concepts.description: Rajaraja Chola, Rajendra Chola, the Brihadishvara temple, the naval expedition against Srivijaya, public works and decline.
concepts.idea: The Cholas built a powerful empire and navy and connected India with Southeast Asia and China.
concepts.rule: The Cholas had Thanjavur, Gangaikondacholapuram and Kanchi as capitals. Rajaraja Chola, from 985, ruled about three decades and conquered parts of Karnataka and Andhra, the 'islands of the sea' (identified as the Maldives) and northern Sri Lanka including Anuradhapura. He built the Brihadishvara temple at Thanjavur and allowed a Buddhist vihara at Nagapattinam for Srivijaya's ruler. Rajendra Chola I ruled nearly 30 years, conquered parts of Odisha and Bengal, took the title Gangaikondachola and built a temple at Gangaikondacholapuram. His 1025 naval expedition against Srivijaya, over control of the Strait of Malacca on the China trade route, defeated its forces and captured the capital but did not occupy it. The Cholas built roads, tanks, wells, canals and lakes. Wars with the Western Chalukyas, Pandyas and Sri Lankan rulers drained the treasury, and the Pandyas absorbed the empire by the 13th century.
concepts.example: Trade with China thrived under the Cholas and Rajendra sent a diplomatic mission there.

concepts.name: The Paramaras and Bhoja
concepts.description: The Paramaras of Malwa, Bhoja Paramara as a scholar-king, Bhojtal and the Bhojeshwar temple.
concepts.idea: Bhoja Paramara was a scholar-king who built lakes, temples and supported learning.
concepts.rule: The Paramaras were vassals of the Pratiharas and Rashtrakutas who became independent in Malwa in the second half of the 10th century with capital Dhara (Dhar). Bhoja Paramara ruled from 1010 for almost half a century, extended his kingdom from Konkan to parts of Rajasthan and sent forces to help the Hindu Shahis against Mahmud. He should not be confused with Bhoja of the Pratiharas. He founded Bhojpur and built a vast lake by harnessing several rivers, of which a part, Bhojtal, remains near Bhopal; the name Bhopal comes from Bhojpal. He built the unfinished Bhojeshwar temple. He supported scholars and wrote on architecture (Samarangana Sutradhara), governance, Sanskrit poetics, medicine and a commentary on the Yogasutras. After his death in 1055 the Paramaras declined.
concepts.example: A local proverb says, 'If there is a lake, it is Bhopal's lake; all others are just ponds'.

concepts.name: The Ghurids: Tarain, Prithviraj and the fall of Nalanda
concepts.description: Muhammad Ghuri, the battles of Tarain, Prithviraj III, Qutb-ud-din Aibak, Bakhtiyar Khilji and the destruction of centres of learning.
concepts.idea: Muhammad Ghuri sought lasting conquest, and his commanders destroyed centres of learning like Nalanda.
concepts.rule: The Ghaznavids declined and the chiefs of Ghur took Ghazni. Their leader Muhammad Ghuri attacked Gujarat but was defeated by the Chaulukyas, with a chronicle crediting a queen leading the army with her son. The Chahamanas (Chauhans) of Ajayameru (Ajmer) held Delhi (Dhillika) and Haryana. Prithviraj III defeated Muhammad Ghuri at Tarain in 1191, but in the Second Battle of Tarain in 1192 Muhammad defeated and executed him. Unlike Mahmud, Muhammad sought territorial conquest and left commanders such as Qutb-ud-din Aibak, who later founded the Delhi Sultanate. Bakhtiyar Khilji conquered Bihar and Bengal, destroying Buddhist monasteries such as Nalanda and Vikramashila; historians agree this hastened Buddhism's decline in India. In 1205 he was defeated in Kamarupa; Muhammad Ghuri and Bakhtiyar died in 1206.
concepts.example: Nalanda's library is said to have burned for months.

concepts.name: Governance, trade, culture and thinkers; taking stock
concepts.description: Administration, economy, culture, Khajuraho, Ramanuja and Basaveshwara, Angkor Wat and the lessons of the period.
concepts.idea: Despite warfare, trade, art and thought flourished and India showed resilience.
concepts.rule: Kingdoms kept large armies and needed efficient administration; Muhammad Ghuri's system was more centralised, granting temporary land assignments to officers for revenue and service. The economy remained agricultural, with crops such as rice, saffron, spices and cotton and irrigation works. The Chalukya king Someshvara III wrote the Manasollasa encyclopaedia. Chandellas built the Kandariya Mahadeva and Lakshmana temples at Khajuraho. Ramanujacharya developed vishishtadvaita vedanta, which sees the world and souls as real and stresses bhakti. Basaveshwara left a minister's post to found the Lingayat movement, rejecting caste distinctions and ritualism, and set up the Anubhava Mandapa. Angkor Wat in Cambodia, built by Suryavarman II in the 12th century, is the largest religious monument in the world. Large parts of north and all of south India stayed outside Turkic rule; the lesson is resilience.
concepts.example: The Anubhava Mandapa let people of all backgrounds meet to discuss life and values.
